title: Notifications: red for every block, and letting the assistant decide "ready"

steps.path: The light on each conversation, on the computer and on your phone
steps.headline: When the assistant's browser asks you something, how should your phone show it?
steps.today: When the browser asks permission (visit a site, buy, send, sign in), the conversation's light stays green, and your phone shows nothing at all; after 90 seconds the browser gives up.
steps.problem: You think the assistant is busy while it is actually waiting on you. On the phone you can't even answer: the browser runs on the computer.
steps.proposal: On the computer it turns red with the usual chime. The question is the phone.

options.label: Red, plus a note
pros: You learn it's waiting wherever you are.
The note tells you why you can't answer it there.
cons: A red you can't act on from the phone.

options.label: Red on the computer only
pros: The phone never shows red you can't act on.
cons: Away from the computer, you never find out; it times out.

steps.headline: Should Claude Code's on-screen dialogs turn the light red?
steps.today: Dialogs like "Usage limit reached", "Message flagged", "Switch model?" and the first-run setup questions show as cards in the chat, but the light stays green or turns amber.
steps.problem: The conversation is stopped until you answer, but nothing says so.
steps.proposal: Treat any unanswered dialog card like a question card: red and the chime, on both screens. Pop-ups the app can't read (it already blocks sending while one is up) count too.

options.label: All of them red
pros: Red always means "it's waiting on you", no exceptions to learn.
cons: "Usage limit reached" goes red even when the only answer is waiting.

options.label: Only ones with a real choice
pros: Red only when you can actually decide something.
cons: Usage limit and similar stay green, so you may not notice it stopped.
A rule you'd have to remember.

steps.path: Conversations with cloud models and big local models
steps.headline: If the assistant finishes while you're away and does NOT notify you, what should its light show?
steps.today: The app turns it blue ("Response ready") on its own whenever a reply finishes while you're looking elsewhere.
steps.problem: You want the assistant, not the app, to decide what is worth your attention. But if it forgets, something has to show.
steps.proposal: Small local models keep today's automatic blue either way. This is about every other session.

options.label: Gray: trust the assistant
pros: Blue only ever means the assistant has something for you.
No false alarms when it stops just to wait on its helpers.
cons: When it forgets, you won't know it finished until you look.

options.label: A quiet "Finished"
pros: Nothing is ever lost: a forgotten one still says it stopped.
Blue still only means "the assistant flagged this".
cons: One more state to tell apart (a gray light with the word Finished).

steps.path: How we find out whether the assistant notifies reliably
steps.headline: How should we switch cloud-model sessions over?
steps.today: Nothing is switched yet; your real app has the old automatic blue.
steps.problem: We don't yet know how often each assistant forgets to notify, or notifies too much.
steps.proposal: Every option starts with about 20 scripted conversations in the test copy (free, normal usage on your account).

options.label: Switch, and keep score
pros: You feel the real thing right away.
A hidden log compares it with the old behaviour on every reply, so after a week we have numbers.
cons: For that week, a forgotten notification really is missed (unless Q-3 is "Finished").

options.label: Score first, switch later
pros: Nothing changes for you until the numbers are in.
cons: You don't feel the new behaviour for a week.
Assistants notify the same either way, so the score is just as good.

steps.path: The harness evaluator, which runs real assistants against scripted cases
steps.headline: Run the paid test across several cloud models?
steps.today: The evaluator can run the same ten situations (finished while away, checkpoint, waiting on helpers, quick answer…) against Claude, GPT, Gemini and a big local model, three times each, and score misses, noise and label quality.
steps.problem: Your own week of use mostly covers the models you use; a model you don't use could be bad at this and we'd never know.
steps.proposal: A free practice run first shows the exact cost. The real run stops at a spending limit you set, and needs a key file you create for it.

options.label: Yes, with a cap
pros: Numbers for every model before anyone else's app depends on it.
cons: Costs money (estimate shown before it runs).

options.label: Not now
pros: Free; your week of use answers it for the models you use.
cons: Other models go untested until someone reports a problem.
